title: Org chart roll-up into reporting_lines
summary: A recursive CTE walks the employee hierarchy down from every VP, a second CTE pulls in contractors, the two are stacked with UNION ALL, and the combined set is written into reporting_lines.
sql:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, e.name, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees e
    WHERE e.title = 'VP'
  UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, e.name, c.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
    WHERE c.depth < 6
),
contractors AS (
  SELECT c.id, c.agency_manager_id AS manager_id, c.name, 1 AS depth
  FROM contractors_raw c
  WHERE c.ended_at IS NULL
)
INSERT INTO reporting_lines (id, manager_id, name, depth)
SELECT * FROM chain
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM contractors
RETURNING id, depth

nodes.label: employees e
nodes.detail: Base table for the recursion's seed query.

nodes.label: WHERE e.title = 'VP'
nodes.plain: Keeps only the VPs — the roots of the walk.
nodes.detail: The anchor (seed) member of the recursive CTE. Everything the recursion finds hangs off these rows.
nodes.delta_note: 38 VPs become the 38 starting rows of the recursion.

nodes.label: UNION ALL
nodes.plain: Stacks the seed rows and every recursive round.
nodes.detail: In a recursive CTE, `UNION ALL` is what feeds each round's output back in. Rows accumulate here: the working table is re-run until a round returns nothing.
nodes.delta_note: 38 seed rows plus roughly 9.400 rows found across 5 recursive rounds.

nodes.label: employees e
nodes.plain: Re-reads employees for the recursive step.
nodes.detail: Each round joins the working table back to `employees` to find the next layer of reports.
nodes.sql_span:
FROM employees e
    JOIN chain c

nodes.label: JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
nodes.plain: Matches each employee to a manager already found.
nodes.detail: This join is what walks one level down the tree per round. One manager row can match many employees, so this is the step where the row count grows.
nodes.sql_span: JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
nodes.delta_note: Per round: each already-found manager pulls in its direct reports (≈4.9 on average).

nodes.label: WHERE c.depth < 6
nodes.plain: Stops the walk after six levels.
nodes.detail: The depth guard is the recursion's termination condition. Without it, a cycle in `manager_id` would loop forever — Postgres has no built-in recursion limit.
nodes.delta_note: Cuts the branches that already reached level 6.

nodes.label: RECURSIVE: chain
nodes.detail: `chain` holds every employee reachable from a VP within six levels, each row carrying its depth.

nodes.label: contractors_raw c
nodes.detail: A separate source that is not part of the employee tree.

nodes.label: WHERE c.ended_at IS NULL
nodes.plain: Keeps contractors whose engagement is still open.
nodes.detail: `IS NULL` is the right test here: `ended_at <> ...` would silently drop every open engagement, because a comparison against NULL is never true.
nodes.delta_note: 2.490 contractors have an end date and are excluded.

nodes.label: UNION ALL
nodes.plain: Stacks employees and contractors into one list.
nodes.detail: `UNION ALL` keeps duplicates, so an employee who also appears as a contractor will land in `reporting_lines` twice. Plain `UNION` would de-duplicate but cost a full sort.
nodes.delta_note: The only step here that adds rows: 9.450 + 610.

nodes.label: INSERT INTO reporting_lines (id, manager_id, name, depth)
nodes.plain: Writes the combined rows into reporting_lines.
nodes.detail: Column order matters: the `SELECT *` feeding this insert must line up positionally with `(id, manager_id, name, depth)`. Adding a column to either side later will break it silently.

nodes.label: RETURNING id, depth
nodes.plain: Hands back the ids and depths just written.
nodes.detail: Avoids a second query to see what was inserted.

funnel.why: Every employee row is the starting point.
Each round adds the direct reports of the rows found in the previous round — this is the one step that multiplies.
A separate branch, filtered to open engagements.
9.450 employees stacked on 610 contractors, duplicates kept.
Every row that reaches the INSERT is written.

notes: Row counts here are reasoned estimates from an average span of control of ~4.9, not measured — run each stage as `SELECT count(*)` to confirm.
`UNION ALL` between chain and contractors keeps duplicates: anyone present in both lists is inserted twice.
The recursion's only guard is `depth < 6`. A cycle in `manager_id` would be capped by that guard, but would still produce wrong rows.
